extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of moral philosophy; readers of Kant's Groundwork
extracted.subtask_description: Close analytic exposition of Kantian practical reason: what constitutes moral feeling, duty, respect, and the a priori grounds of moral obligation. Focuses on distinguishing actions done from duty (moral worth) from those done from inclination and on the methodological order for a critique of practical reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect as moral feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral feeling (respect) is produced simply by reason; it does not serve to estimate actions or to found the objective moral law, but merely as a motive to make the law a maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect is an effect on the sensibility produced by pure practical reason; it functions as a motive to obedience but not as the foundation of objective moral law. It is non-pathological (not mere pleasure or pain) and can be known a priori insofar as it follows from the conception of the moral law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect applies to persons only
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect is owed to persons, not to things; admiration or astonishment may apply to things, but not respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one admires mountains or talents, but respect (properly speaking) is felt toward persons whose example exhibits a moral law that humbles self-conceit. Fontenelle's saying ('I bow before a great man, but my mind does not bow') contrasts mere external deference with inward respect grounded in moral example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law must be the motive (moral interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a morally good will the law itself must be the motive; the moral interest is a pure interest of practical reason alone, independent of sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A maxim is morally good only if it rests simply on the interest taken in obedience to the law. Any admixture of inclination or self-interest disqualifies the maxim for possessing moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between legality and morality (acting according to duty vs from duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness of having acted according to duty (legality) can occur even when inclinations determined the will; moral worth (morality) exists only when the action is done from duty (from respect for the law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by the subjective principle (motive) of their maxims: only actions determined by respect for the law have true moral worth; mere conformity to law is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral feeling is a priori and non-pathological
rubrics_metrics.description: The feeling of respect is not a pathological feeling (not pleasure or pain) and depends on the conception of a law 'simply as to its form' rather than on any empirical object; it is therefore knowable a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat moral feeling as sense-based inclination. Its a priori character distinguishes pure practical reason from motives grounded in sensible desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty as constraint/obligation for finite beings
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite rational beings, moral necessity is constraint (obligation); actions based on this are duties, not proceedings previously pleasing or spontaneously chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral actions by recognizing that finite creatures require respect for law (which may involve fear or apprehension of transgression) as the subjective principle; this constraint is the proper source of moral action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical love versus pathological love (what can be commanded)
rubrics_metrics.description: A command can require 'practical love' (to like to do the commandments) but cannot command pathological love (an immediate feeling), since liking cannot be produced by a command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret evangelical commands (e.g., 'Love thy neighbour') as prescribing a moral disposition to pursue duties, not as demanding involuntary affections. The law commands the endeavour toward such a disposition, not immediate feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: moral fanaticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral fanaticism is the deliberate overstepping of the bounds of practical reason by placing the subjective determining principle of correct actions in anything but the law itself (e.g., in sympathy, self-love, imaginative pride).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating spontaneous nobility or extraordinary feeling as substitutes for duty-based respect; evaluate motives and beware of praising actions when motives are pathological rather than law-based. Examples include sentimental educators or romanticized virtue that confuses inclination with duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personhood/autonomy: treat persons as ends in themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Every rational being is an end in himself; by virtue of autonomy his will must never be used merely as means, but always also as an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect for persons follows from their status as autonomous legislators of the moral law. Moral evaluation requires checking whether actions instrumentally use persons or respect their autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism of moral feeling: humiliation and self-approbation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of the moral law produces humiliation (lowering of self-esteem relative to the law) on the sensible side and an elevation of practical esteem for the law (self-approbation) on the intellectual side; this produces interest in obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand respect as simultaneously a negative effect (humbling) and a positive subjective motive (self-approbation that encourages obedience). This explains how an a priori law can yield a practical motive for finite agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of moral law in personality/freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of the law's authority is personality — freedom and independence from the mechanism of nature — whereby the rational being is subject to pure practical laws given by its own reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground moral obligations in the autonomy of rational agents rather than in contingent natural causes; the dignity of persons and the imperatives of duty derive from this conception of personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral disposition and the aim of virtue versus holiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper moral condition for creatures is virtue (a moral disposition militant: obeying from duty), not holiness (a hypothetical perfect love that would remove duty as command); love of the law is an idealally desirable but unattainable goal for creatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral character by whether one maintains duty-respect as motive in ordinary fallible human life; beware of conflating moral perfection (holiness) with the attainable moral disposition (virtue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological order for Analytic of pure practical reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The critical examination of practical reason must begin with the possibility of practical principles a priori, then proceed to concepts of objects of practical reason (absolute good/evil), and conclude with the relation of pure practical reason to sensibility (moral sentiment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing moral theory, do not start from intuition or empirical sensibility; begin from a priori principles (the moral principle), then subsume possible actions, and finally consider the influence on feeling. This reverses the order of the theoretical analytic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: doctrine of happiness (empirical) vs doctrine of morality (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of happiness is grounded entirely in empirical principles, whereas the doctrine of morality does not admit empirical principles into its foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating motives or moral arguments, separate empirical incentives (pleasure/pain, useful consequences) from a priori moral principles. Moral evaluation must exclude empirical principles from the foundational law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for empirical admixture in practical motives (analytic experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can test whether a will is empirically determined by adding the moral law as a determining principle: empirical principles will 'forsake' their hold when the moral law is added (analogy with a chemical precipitation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thought-experiment style tests on maxims: present the agent with the moral law added to their empirically motivated will; if the empirical motive yields to the law (i.e., is detected as distinct), the admixture is empirical and not pure.
